GOLDMAN SACHS
SUMMER ANALYST
INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE 2023
SAILIE GHOLE
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
Batch 2025

-
PRE-PLACEMENT TALK (PPT)
[DATE : 7th August, 2023]
Platform: Zoom Webinar
About: Goldman Sachs is a global investment banking and financial services firm. It offers
a wide range of financial services, including investment banking, asset management, and
securities trading, serving clients that range from individuals to large corporations and
governments. Goldman Sachs is known for its expertise in financial markets, its
commitment to innovation, and its global presence in major financial hubs around the
world.
During this Pre-Placement Talk meet, you’ll learn about the company's work, current
projects, work environment, their internship programme and guiding principles.
Listening carefully during this talk is important because what you learn here might come
up in your interviews.
ONLINE TEST
[DATE : 8th August, 2023]
Participants: All 200+ third-year students who applied for Goldman Sachs were
shortlisted for the online test.
Test Platform: Hackerrank - video, and screen proctored.
Test duration: 60 mins
No. of sections: 2
Total no. of questions: 14

-
Section 1: Aptitude, CS Fundamentals and DSA questions section.
[Time for this section: 50 mins, No. of questions: 12 (10 Mcqs and 2 coding questions) ]
●
First 10 mcq questions were a mix of aptitude and cs fundamentals mostly from
data structures, oops, os ,dbms and few debugging/output-related questions.
Question 1-10:
+5 - 2 marking scheme
The topics of questions which I remember from the MCQs section are as follows:
i) Huffman coding
ii) Permutation and combination
iii) AVL trees
iv) Preorder traversal of binary search tree of the given order of numbers.
v) Stack based implementation of Infix to postfix conversion: which option require max
memory allocation
vi) Debugging some python code
vii) A Resource Allocation Graph
Tip: Mark only those questions about which you are sure as there is a -2 for every
incorrect answer.
●
Next two were coding questions.
Question 11: Sum of magic parent nodes in a tree.
In this tree, a node is called a magic parent node if one immediate child of the node is a
factor of the other immediate child. A node having only one immediate child can never
be a magic parent node.
Output: Sum of all magic parent nodes in the tree

-
Example:
Ans: 146
Here 4 and 142 both are magic nodes.
Function to be completed (this is what I remember, it might be not exact):
public static int findMagicParentNodesSum(int n, int rootValue, String[] pos, int[] val) {
}
There is an array passed named String[] pos which contains the position of other nodes
with respect to Root and also an array Int[] Val which contains the data of nodes of
corresponding index value in pos.
Solution: I wrote a recursive function that traverses the tree, checking at each node if it
qualifies as a "magic parent node" according to the criteria provided and also checking if
the current node is a leaf node, if it is, then it cannot be a magic node since and hence
return 0;. If a node meets the criteria, its value is added to a running sum. Finally, the
function returns this sum, representing the sum of all magic parent nodes in the tree.
Refer these similar question with different condition for a node to be magic parent tree:
https://leetcode.com/discuss/interview-question/901547/goldman-sachs-sde-2020
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/count-of-nodes-in-a-binary-tree-with-immediate-childre
n-as-its-factors/
I spent most of my time on this question because I kept encountering an in-built I/O
exception error. Eventually, I decided to comment out the lines that were causing the
error, which resolved the issue. However, my code produced the wrong answer. It became
clear that I didn't have a proper understanding of how to navigate the tree using position
and value arrays. At that point, I realised I had already invested a significant amount of

-
time in this question and decided to move on to the next one, as it appeared more
manageable.
Question 12: Count X and Y in a grid
An N x N matrix (say A) consists alternating ‘X’ and ‘Y’. There will be a list of queries. Each
query is an array of size 3 ([a, b, c]). The first term represents the query type. The next two
terms b and c represent the index of elements in the matrix.
The first query (a = 1) requires us to change the element at A[b][c] to ‘Y’.
The second query (a = 2) requires us to change the element at A[b][c] to ‘X’.
The third query (a = 3) requires us to print the matrix whose top left corner is A[b][c] and
bottom right corner is the end of the matrix (i.e, A[N-1][N-1])
Example:
Function to be completed(this is what I remember, it might be not exact):
public static void countXandY(int N, int Q, char str[], int x1[] , int y1[] ) {
}

-
str, x1 and y1 are arrays that hold the Q inputs. Q is the length of the 3 arrays.
str contains X, Y and C characters. In the grid for (x,y) x1 contains the value for row and y1
contains the value for column.
Solution: This question was pretty straightforward.Firstly make a N x N character grid and
initialise it with alternate Xs and Ys.Start a loop from 0 to Q. If str[i] == ‘X’ fill the position
grid[x1[i]-1][y1[i]-1] with ‘X’. Similarly for Y and when str[i]==’C’ simply count the number
of X and Y in the grid from grid[x1[i]-1][y1[i]-1] to grid[n-1][n-1] and print them.
All 12/12 test cases were passed.
Section 2: Tell us about yourself section (Subjective questions)
[Time for this section: 10 mins, No. of questions: 2 ]
Question 13: Your team is working on an important project, and a teammate has an urgent
personal matter and needs to stop working. What would you do to manage the situation
and ensure the project's progress?
Question 14: Share a memorable project experience from your past, one that left a lasting
impression on you. What made it stand out the most to you?
The results were announced two days prior to the interview. As soon as I received the
email, I felt a mix of happiness and nervousness since it was going to be my first interview.
One of my seniors provided me with encouragement and advised me to give it my best
shot. I started by reviewing all the previous year Goldman Sachs interview experiences. I
went through past interview coding questions on platforms like LeetCode/Gfg (
https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/goldman-sachs-interview-preparation/), and I dedicated
time revising CS fundamentals, with a special focus on DBMS and OOPs and also
implementation of all data structures and their operations.

-
INTERVIEW ROUND 1
[DATE : 23rd August, 2023]
Participants: From the online test, 13 students (4 girls and 9 boys) were shortlisted for
the Interview.
Platform: Zoom and Hackerrank CodePair
ROUND 1: Technical Interview (30 mins)
I joined the meet 10 mins before the said timing with the given meetingId and passcode.
After 15-20 mins,I was directed to a breakout room where my interviewer greeted me
warmly, initiating the conversation saying "Hey Sailie, how are you doing?". We proceeded
to introduce ourselves, with him sharing insights about his background for about 4-5
minutes, followed by my own introduction. (Have some pointers ready in your mind to
answer this question as this part is very important. Based on your introduction, the
interviewer might ask you certain questions). He appreciated my introduction which made
me feel comfortable and confident.
During my introduction, I mentioned my ongoing learning about MongoDB, so he started
asking questions about it. What is MongoDB, what type of database it is? Is it a SQL or
NoSQL database? What is the difference between SQL or NoSQL databases? Do you
know about ACID properties? Then the conversation shifted to Firebase as it was
mentioned in my resume. What is a firebase? What type of database is it? How do we
authenticate users using firebase? I was able to answer all of them.
Another question he asked me was which is my favourite subject? I said data structures.
Then he asked me why data structures and which one is your favourite? I answered this
using real-life examples of data structures and for my favourite data structure I answered
stack. Then he asked him what are stack and queues? I explained both and their operations
using examples. Further he asked what is a deque and how can we implement it? I
explained deque and its implementation using array as well as linked list.

-
He moved on to the programming language I prefer, and I answered Java. On that he
asked, why java? Give some inbuilt functions in java.Moving on to operating systems he
asked, which operating system does your laptop have? Which other operating systems
have I worked on? What is the difference you have observed between linux and windows?
I gave him all the answers.
Then he told me to open the hackerrank codepair link (The site where the interviewer and
candidate can code on the same IDE) and further typed the question.
Question: An array of strings is given containing timings in Railway time or 24-Hour
format. We have to find the closest timings.
Example: Input: Array- [ 1:30, 4:30, 22:45, 23:00 ]
Output: 15 mins , [22:45, 23:00]
Solution: We will firstly convert all the timings in string 24-hr format to minutes of integer
datatype ( eg: 22 * 60 + 45 mins for 22:45 ). Then we will sort that array. (Here he asked
me about sorting algorithms and their complexities). Then we will run a loop to find the
minimum difference between two consecutives numbers in the array.
He was satisfied with my approach and told me to code it. I was able to code it correctly.
Then he said “Great, I’m done from my side, do you have any questions?”
I asked him 2 questions. Firstly I asked, will my present knowledge be useful if I get
selected. Secondly, how I could make the most of the internship programme.
He answered my questions very nicely and said “You may leave the room now, hope to see
you soon. All the best.” This ending sentence made me feel positive about my 1st round.
Key Takeaways from this round:-
●
Think loud, and always communicate your approach to the interviewer
continuously. He might give you hints if you get stuck somewhere.
●
Be thorough with the techstack you mention in your resume and introduction.
●
You must thoroughly revise CS fundamentals.
●
We should approach the interview as a discussion rather than a mere
question-and-answer session to relieve interview nerves.

-
INTERVIEW ROUND 2
[DATE : 23rd August, 2023]
Participants: From the 1st round, 7 students (2 girls and 5 boys) were shortlisted for the
2nd round of Interview.
Platform: Zoom
ROUND 2: Technical Interview (35-40 mins)
I was sent to the waiting room after the first round, and after about 15-20 minutes, I was
directed to the second breakout room where my interviewer was already waiting. He
introduced himself and began with the classic interview opener, "Tell me about yourself." I
provided an introduction, and from there, the interview proceeded with a series of
questions. (This interview was characterised by a wide range of questions and in-depth
discussions here and there, I don't remember the exact flow and format of all the
questions, so just listing down what all I remember and my answers , I am not sure
whether they are completely accurate.)
The interview began with a question about my programming language preference, to
which I responded that I prefer Java. Following that, the interviewer asked me a series of
questions related to object-oriented programming (OOP):
What are interfaces in java?
-
Interfaces are blueprints for classes that define method signatures without
implementations.
What is the difference between interface and abstract classes?
-
Interfaces provide full abstraction and allow multiple inheritance, whereas abstract
classes can have method implementations and support single inheritance.
Can we create objects of interfaces and abstract classes?
-
Objects cannot be created directly from interfaces or abstract classes, we need
concrete classes that implement or extend them.
Can we declare functions with the same name in abstract classes or interfaces?

-
-
Yes, we can declare functions with the same name in abstract classes and
interfaces, but they must be implemented in the concrete classes that inherit or
implement them.
Further, he presented me with a sentence related to abstract classes, interfaces, and
multiple classes. He asked whether the sentence was correct or incorrect. Initially, I had
difficulty understanding the question and took some time to comprehend it. Despite my
efforts, I wasn't entirely certain about the answer. At this point, I started to feel a bit
nervous, but I made a conscious effort to remain calm and respond to the best of my
ability. I provided my answer, but the interviewer indicated that it was incorrect. However,
he reassured me by saying, "No problem".
Moving ahead he asked, what happens when you compile a Java code?
-
When we compile Java code, it goes through a process that translates the
human-readable Java code into machine-language code.
On that he smiled and asked machine-language code or bytecode?
-
They are the same. Machine understandable code is a lower-level binary format
called bytecode containing 0s and 1s.
How can a java code running on your machine, can run on my machine?
-
Due to Java-Virtual Machines. The bytecode is a platform-independent
representation of the Java code and it can then be executed by the Java Virtual
Machine (JVM) on different platforms, making Java a cross-platform programming
language.
What is the difference between a JVM and a compiler?
-
A JVM (Java Virtual Machine) executes Java bytecode, while a compiler translates
human-readable source code into bytecode.
What are APIs?
-
Application Programming Interfaces which allow different software to talk to each
other (and further explained more about the process of how programs get
information from another program).
-
What is JSON?
-
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text-based format that uses key-value pairs
to represent data in a structured form,

-
What is hashing?
-
Hashing is a process of converting data (like strings or numbers) into a fixed-size
string of characters, typically a hash code (here I gave an example of hashing in
passwords).
What is a hashmap and how would you implement it?
-
A hashmap is a data structure that stores key-value pairs, allowing efficient
retrieval and storage of values by their associated keys.
-
To implement it, use an array where each element is a linked list or an array, and a
hash function to map keys to specific array indices.
How can hashmaps be used in the real world?
-
Data retrieval systems like dictionaries.
Random ID generator -> How can a XYZ company develop a system to generate unique
order IDs for all orders in India, considering that each user may place multiple orders on
different days, and the goal is to ensure each order can be uniquely identified?
-
I took a while to come up with an approach. Then I gave him 1 random approach on
which he replied think more. This discussion went on for like 10 -12 mins.
Then I said the following approach.
-> If The order is from Mumbai, supposedly from XYZ person on 10/9/23
15 bits:
MUM100923000001
3 bits for city + 6 bits for date + 6 random digits
This can give
We will store this in a database (maybe in a hashmap: key as unique ID and value as
customer details) to check for duplicates and track order details.
For every order and last 6 digits will be unique factor
He commented, "This is decent, but think more." I paused to consider the question
further, but regrettably, I couldn't generate an alternative answer. In response, he said,
"No problem." I then politely inquired about the approach he had in mind, and he kindly
suggested that I could explore the question further after the interview.
Then the conversation shifted to data structures.

-
Have you played snake and ladder? What data structure can we use to implement it?
-
Graphs
How can you implement it using graphs?
-
Using BFS approach
Further he asked why bfs and what else will you need for its implementation. I told him my
approach. He seemed satisfied with my answer and moved on to the next question.
(This snake and ladder question was repeated for most of the candidates)
You can refer to this.
Give some real life examples of graph data structure.
-
Flight Routes, GPS, Social Networks (explained them with real-life scenarios).
Then he started going through my resume and started asking firebase questions.
-
About Firebase.
-
About key-value databases.
-
What is RDBMS? RDBMS and Nosql difference?
After that, he inquired if I had any idea about design patterns. My response was, "No, I
haven't gone through them yet." At this point, he mentioned that our allotted time for the
interview had come to an end and asked if I had any questions for him. I took the
opportunity to inquire once more about the abstract and interface true or false question
that had initially confused me. In response, he smiled and kindly provided the correct
answer. I thanked him and assured him that I would make sure to review that concept
thoroughly.
Then I asked him, what is his review on my resume?
On which he answered that the resume doesn’t matter to him, what matters is crystal
clear clarity on concepts (When I heard that, I started to worry if at all he thought I didn't
understand the concepts well, and it made me a little nervous about the second round.)
Then I smiled, said thank you, he replied all the best and this marked the end of my 2nd
interview round.

-
Key Takeaways from this round:-
1. During an interview, remember that not every question or situation will be
straightforward. There may be moments where you feel stuck and can’t think
further. In such situations, maintain your composure and communicate your
thoughts, whatever you are thinking about the solution.
2. Even though the interviewer will disagree with your solution or may not
understand it. Don't ever try to debate with him or override him to prove your
point.
3. You must be thorough with your chosen programming language and oops.
4. This interviewer was asking 2 to 3 questions combined in a single question. So it's
important to listen to the whole question properly, keeping pointers in mind and
seeking clarification when needed.
CONCLUSION
All seven candidates were waiting in the waiting room after the second round.
Subsequently, two students were selected one by one to proceed to the third round, while
the remaining five of us were awaiting our turn. After an hour had passed, the HR
representative joined us in the waiting room and conveyed that they had completed their
interviews for the day. We were instructed to leave the meeting, with the assurance that
they would email the results shortly. All five of us left the meeting, under the assumption
that the two candidates who had advanced to the third round were the ones selected.
At around 2:30 p.m, the results were mailed and 3 students (1 girl and 2 boys ) were
selected. Fortunately, I was the girl selected, and was filled with happiness and gratitude.

-

PREPARATION TIPS
1) Participate in LeetCode contests to practise and enhance your problem-solving
speed. You can also try solving ‘leetcode daily question’ everyday.
2) Revise the CS fundamentals (OS, OOPS, DBMS).
If time permits go through CN and low/high level design concepts.
3) Go through important interview questions based on your chosen programming
language. (For JAVA: link)
4) Prepare a nice introduction and also go through behavioural questions asked
during the HR round (link).
5) Know your resume very well. Go through questions based on your project
techstack (example: firebase, mongodb, react, etc ) from interview bit or GFG.
6) Know your projects well, use the STAR method to explain your project and your
contribution in it (if it's a team project).
7) There's a wide array of resources available, so it's essential not to get overwhelmed
with choices. Simply start your preparation and go with the ones that you find most
understandable and effective for your learning style.
8) Everyday try to do at least one to two questions, don't break the flow , it becomes
quite difficult to get back on track.
9) Read previous year interview experiences (trust me they help a lot).
10) Engage in discussions with your friends about different questions and approaches;
you may discover new questions/approaches that you weren't previously familiar
with.
11) Avoid comparing your preparation progress with others. Focus on your own
growth and trust your journey.
12) When you feel demotivated or anxious about the outcome, remind yourself to
concentrate solely on your preparation. Trust that with dedication and effort,
things will fall into place, and you'll achieve what you've worked for! : )
ALL THE BEST!!
